```{r disc-stability, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
.dstab <- read_result("consensus_endpoint_stats")
.drng  <- function(v) sprintf("%.2f--%.2f", min(v), max(v))
.dsl   <- .drng(.dstab$vs_reported$loading[, "median"])
.dsj   <- .drng(.dstab$vs_reported$top_jaccard[, "median"])
.dsnt  <- as.integer(.dstab$meta$ntop)
```

DeSurv allows patient survival to shape gene-program discovery, yielding a tumor--stroma architecture that connects prognostic information with interpretable malignant and stromal programs. The practical value lies in what that architecture yields, program-specific gene lists that can be compared with established classifications and investigated biologically across cohorts. In PDAC, the architecture comprised a dominant survival-aligned program, D1, characterized by coordinated cross-patient variation in classical tumor and restCAF-like stromal features, alongside separately resolved proCAF-like stromal and basal-like tumor programs. D1 remained prognostic after adjustment for the established PurIST and DeCAF classifications, and was supported on its classical tumor side by GATA6 RNA in situ hybridization. The frozen programs then transferred without refitting across four independent external patient cohorts.

This difference in the recovered programs persisted when rank and tuning effort were matched. An unsupervised control at $\alpha = 0$, matched to DeSurv on rank, optimizer, tuning budget and consensus initialization and tuned on cross-validated concordance, did not recover D1. A rank-optimized unsupervised control recovered comparable prognostic information across a broader seven-factor representation, and conventional supervised predictors produced scores aligned with the dominant prognostic direction, correlating only weakly with the separately resolved proCAF-like program (Fig.\ \ref{fig:val}b). These comparisons separate prognostic information from the representation in which that information is recovered.

This distinction also clarifies the role of the frozen gene-program basis. When programs are learned without outcome information, their prognostic relevance is assessed after discovery. In DeSurv, survival acts directly on the gene-program matrix $W$ while the reconstruction objective requires the learned programs to continue representing the observed transcriptome. Once learned, the gene weights are held fixed, so external validation tests the same programs rather than a newly estimated representation. In CoxNMF and SurvNMF, the survival term depends on sample-side latent representations [@huang2020low; @le2025survnmf]. In DeSurv, it depends directly on projections through the gene-program matrix, and new samples are scored using fixed gene weights without an additional sample-loading estimation step (Supplementary Table \ref{tab:architecture}). Empirically, supervision reorganized rather than replaced the reconstruction-driven structure. D2 and D3 corresponded closely to the major stromal and tumor factors recovered by standard NMF, whereas D1 was poorly reconstructable from those matched-rank factors.

Program-level outputs are the practical product of this architecture, because the genes assigned to a program determine how it is interpreted and what is tested next. Previous PDAC studies illustrate how interpretable malignant and stromal programs can support biological characterization and the development of single-sample classifiers [@moffitt2015virtual; @peng2019novo; @rashid2020purity; @peng2024determination]. Program-specific gene lists connect measured scores to biological annotation and provide candidates for subsequent classifier development. DeSurv extends this line of work by allowing patient outcomes to influence the gene weights themselves, and D2 remains available as separately measurable proCAF-like stromal context although the fitted risk score combines D1 and D3. Such outputs supply candidate signatures and hypotheses for biological investigation and biomarker development, without yet establishing clinical utility or a treatment-selection rule.

Rank choice and initialization can affect the recovered gene programs, and both were examined here. Standard NMF criteria gave conflicting rank choices in the PDAC training data, and increasing rank progressively broadened correspondence to established PDAC programs. The three-factor DeSurv solution and the seven-factor unsupervised control were selected by the same one-standard-error rule, and seven is the smallest rank within one standard error of the best configuration in the $\alpha = 0$ search, so the two differ in representation size rather than marking a minimum-rank requirement for either method. Survival supervision provides an outcome-informed criterion for shaping the representation, but it does not remove the non-uniqueness of matrix factorization, and individual DeSurv runs from different random starts recover appreciably different gene sets. Consensus fits built from disjoint halves of the same cached restart pool agreed closely with the reported basis (gene-loading correlation `r .dsl`, top-`r .dsnt` Jaccard `r .dsj`; Supplementary Information, Stability of the recovered gene programs). This supports stability to restart-pool composition within the training data, while leaving reproducibility under independent repetition, and the stability of the full consensus procedure under patient resampling, to be established.

The simulations identify conditions under which survival information improves program recovery. In the primary setting, the marker genes defining the prognostic program contributed less expression variation than shared background genes excluded from the survival-generating gene set. DeSurv recovered those prognostic markers more accurately than its unsupervised limit. In the mixed setting, the benefit differed between program-specific markers and shared background genes, while test-set concordance was near chance for both methods under the null. These findings provide a controlled example of how survival supervision can prioritize prognostically relevant structure that contributes relatively little expression variation.

Three statistical qualifications bound the prognostic findings. DeSurv uses a proportional-hazards objective, while the external validation data showed attenuation of the prognostic association over follow-up (Results), so the reported hazard ratios are time-averaged summaries and extensions could accommodate non-proportional hazards or nonlinear survival relationships. The integrated Brier analysis recalibrated the score's scalar slope and baseline hazard within each validation dataset, so it describes apparent prediction error rather than out-of-sample prediction error (Supplementary Information, Proper-scoring sensitivity of the external validation). The pooled training objective was fitted without a cohort term; within-cohort analyses argued against simple encoding of training-cohort membership, though cohort influence on the learned representation remains possible (Supplementary Information, Cohort handling in the training objective).

The question DeSurv addresses extends beyond PDAC. In any tumor type, the programs that dominate expression variation may differ from those most relevant to survival, so outcome information could help prioritize programs that reconstruction alone underweights. Testing generalizability will require multi-cancer evaluation of prognostic performance, program recovery and stability, with attention to cohort composition and event counts. Comparators should include unsupervised decompositions and strong penalized-regression baselines, which remain difficult to outperform consistently for out-of-sample prognosis [@smith2020standard]. PDAC is the empirical demonstration presented here rather than evidence of pan-cancer validation.

In treated cohorts the frozen scores remained informative in exploratory analyses. In O'Kane/COMPASS, D1 remained prognostic in an analysis stratified by treatment arm, although arm-level sample sizes limited assessment of variation in the association across treatments, and the epithelial-enriched profiles support transport of its tumor-associated component in particular. The increase in the projected D2 score after treatment in the Linehan cohort indicates a shift toward proCAF-associated bulk expression, which may reflect altered cellular composition, transcriptional state or both, and does not establish a treatment-induced change in fibroblast state. Whether these programs predict differential treatment benefit therefore remains unresolved and will require adequately powered, prespecified treatment-by-program interaction analyses in studies designed to support treatment comparisons.

The tumor--stroma architecture described here is a bulk-tissue phenomenon. It reflects cross-patient covariation in tumor- and stroma-associated transcriptional programs rather than cellular co-expression or spatial adjacency within individual tumors. Within it, D1 is the dominant survival-aligned program rather than the architecture itself, and this organization is consistent with broader evidence that malignant lineage state and stromal composition vary together in PDAC [@ogawa2020stroma; @neuzillet2022periostin; @lee2024tumorcaf]. The restCAF-like and proCAF-like labels denote correspondence to reference signatures rather than direct resolution of single-cell CAF states. Adjustment for PurIST and DeCAF supports D1's prognostic association beyond those classifiers, purity adjustment in the PACA-AU datasets leaves the risk score's association essentially unchanged, and other supervised methods recover a related patient-score direction. GATA6 RNA in situ hybridization independently supports D1's classical tumor component; these analyses do not establish the cellular identity of its stromal component. Single-cell or spatial profiling could clarify the cellular sources of these programs; linking those sources to prognosis would additionally require outcome-annotated cohorts and scoring methods appropriate for the measurement platform.

In PDAC, incorporating survival during factorization recovered a three-program tumor--stroma architecture that transferred across independent cohorts while retaining biological components that could be interrogated separately. More generally, DeSurv provides a framework for asking not only whether transcriptomic data predict outcome, but which biological programs are recovered when outcome information helps shape their discovery.
